clue.text: We hear companion for dining is having a grouse

indicators.note: what we hear is sound alone, so the spelling may differ from the word meant

blocks.note: 'wining and dining' is the stock pairing, so wining keeps dining company

explanation.surface: Someone at a dinner party complains about the company or the food.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a verb phrase: 'having a grouse' means complaining, and the h is silent in most accents.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a grouse is British slang for to complain, which is exactly what whining describes.

clue.text: Labour, at this time: work on job

blocks.note: OP is short for opus, a work
a position is a job

explanation.surface: A Labour activist busies themselves with work on a job in the present day.
explanation.walkthrough: When this was set the UK Labour Party was out of government, so it was the official Opposition in Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest party not in government in the House of Commons is formally titled His Majesty's Opposition.

clue.text: Youngster driving from here north

blocks.note: golfers drive the ball off the tee
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A young person drives off heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driving' is not motoring but the golf shot from the tee.
explanation.definitionFit: A teen is a teenager, a young person aged thirteen to nineteen.

clue.text: Dancer picked up one-step?

indicators.note: something picked up by the ear is heard, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: one step of a staircase is a stair

explanation.surface: Was this dancer spotted doing the one-step, an old ballroom dance?
explanation.walkthrough: The one-step is a real ragtime dance, which makes the surface plausible; Fred Astaire was the Hollywood dancer.
explanation.definitionFit: Fred Astaire was the most celebrated dancer of classic Hollywood musicals.

clue.text: Unfortunately rejected wish to hug leader of County Mayo's close cousin?

indicators.note: something rejected is thrown back, so the word for unfortunately runs backwards
the leader of a word is its first letter
to hug is to wrap arms around, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: alas is an exclamation meaning unfortunately
a dream is a wish or hope
first letter of County

explanation.surface: An Irish family story: a rejected wish to embrace the head of County Mayo's near relative.
explanation.walkthrough: County Mayo is an Irish county, but here Mayo is short for mayonnaise; salad cream is the tangier British bottled dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: Salad cream is a British bottled condiment closely resembling mayonnaise, so it is mayonnaise's near relation.

clue.text: Sweet kitty raising tail

indicators.note: in a down entry raising the last letter lifts it higher, so it is moved up into the word

blocks.note: a pool is a kitty, a shared fund of money

explanation.surface: A cat with a sweet nature lifts its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: Kitty is a pot of money, not a cat; the last letter of the four moves up one place, and Polo is a British brand of mint sweet with a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: A Polo is a ring-shaped peppermint, a branded sweet sold in Britain.

clue.text: One may treat a poor canine in depression? It's barking

definitions.text: One may treat a poor canine

indicators.note: barking means mad in British slang, so these letters are in a crazy order

blocks.note: a dent is a small depression in a surface
the letters of It's rearranged

explanation.surface: A vet treats a depressed dog, and the dog is barking.
explanation.walkthrough: The canine is a tooth, not a dog; barking is British slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Canines are pointed teeth, and a dentist is the professional who treats a decayed or damaged tooth.

clue.text: Behave cruelly towards e.g. cats and dogs

blocks.note: to whip someone is to treat them cruelly
cats are an example of pets

explanation.surface: A warning against mistreating household animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dogs' looks like the end of a list of pets, but 'and' is only a link and dogs is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Whippets are a breed of slim, fast greyhound-like racing dog.

clue.text: Inspired article about how the Mail sees the Guardian?

indicators.note: about means around, so the article wraps the other piece

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article

blocks.clueFragment: how the Mail sees the Guardian
blocks.note: the right-wing Daily Mail mocks the left-leaning Guardian as woke

explanation.surface: An inspired piece about one newspaper's view of a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mail and the Guardian are British newspapers of right and left; the Mail routinely calls the Guardian woke.
explanation.definitionFit: To be inspired in the sense of stirred into action or awareness is to be awoken or roused.

clue.text: Current mains supply, with no problem at night

indicators.note: read as supple-ly, flexibly, so the letters bend into a new order

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An electrical supply that works without trouble overnight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' reads as a noun but is the adverb from supple; the anagram letters come from both sides of 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: Insomnia is the inability to sleep, a trouble that strikes during the night.

clue.text: Is a surrogate parent plump, and terribly sad about it?

indicators.note: something done terribly is messed up, so the letters are jumbled
about means around, so the jumbled word goes round the chosen word

blocks.note: to plump for something is to opt for it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A surrogate parent who has put on weight feels miserable about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plump' looks like fat, but it is the verb, as in plump for.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who adopts a child takes on the role of parent in place of the birth parents.

clue.text: Milliner suffering with sciatica dismisses one being critical of the cloth

indicators.note: dismissing someone sends them away, so a letter leaves the mix
a sufferer is in a bad way, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one, here removed

explanation.surface: A hat-maker in back pain fires a critic of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: A milliner would deal in cloth, but 'the cloth' here means the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth is an idiom for the clergy, and anticlericalism is opposition to the clergy's influence.

clue.text: Jersey, say, and stockings worn by posh MPs here

indicators.note: clothing worn by someone surrounds them, so the stockings enclose the posh letter

blocks.note: a Jersey is a breed of cow, and a cow is a lower, one that lows
hose is an old word for stockings
U means upper-class in British slang

explanation.surface: Posh MPs turn up in jumpers and stockings.
explanation.walkthrough: A Jersey looks like a jumper, but it is a dairy cow, and a cow lows; U for upper-class is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Commons, where MPs sit, is the lower house of the British Parliament.

clue.text: Canal worker is a hair fetishist?

blocks.note: first meaning: the person who operates the gates on a canal
second meaning, whimsical: one who hangs on to tresses

explanation.walkthrough: Locks are both canal gates and strands of hair, so someone keeping hair locks is jokily the same title; the question mark flags the fanciful second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A lock-keeper runs a canal lock, and the same phrase literally means a collector of hair tresses.

clue.text: Sees Victor wisecracking?

indicators.note: something cracking breaks apart, so the letters come out broken up

blocks.note: Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the first half of the word, wise, is the letters the second half scrambles

explanation.surface: Does someone see a man named Victor making jokes?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wisecracking' must be split: the first half supplies the letters, the second scrambles them.
explanation.definitionFit: To view something is to see or look at it, so views and sees are synonymous verbs.

clue.text: Serenity shown by sport star

blocks.note: PE is physical education, sport at school
an ace is a star performer

explanation.surface: A sports star displays great calm under pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: Peace and serenity are both states of calm free from disturbance.

clue.text: Soft wood frames you heard getting mass approval

indicators.note: heard means only the sound counts, so a single letter can stand for the word
a frame surrounds a picture, so the wood goes round the other piece

blocks.note: poplar is a soft timber
the letter U sounds like you

explanation.surface: A wooden frame that people say is liked by everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Something popular is widely liked, enjoying approval from the masses.

clue.text: A peer who fancies men and women is not quite right

blocks.note: taken as written
bi is short for bisexual
a toff is an upper-class person, the sort a peer is

explanation.surface: A bisexual aristocrat is judged by others as a bit improper.
explanation.walkthrough: A bit off is British idiom for slightly unacceptable or not right; a toff is a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is a bit off means it is somewhat wrong or inappropriate.

clue.text: Persuaded Germany to follow elected fascist leader

blocks.note: a candidate elected is in
Il Duce was Mussolini's title
D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: Germany was talked into following an elected fascist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To follow' places the German letter after the others.
explanation.definitionFit: To induce someone is to persuade or prevail on them to act.

clue.text: Noble with really vacuous birthday celebrations interrupted by family clodhoppers

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of its inside letters
something interrupted has another thing break into its middle

blocks.note: a count is a nobleman
outer letters of really
the bumps is a British custom of tossing a birthday child in the air once per year of age
kin are family

explanation.surface: An aristocrat with dreadfully empty-headed birthday parties, gatecrashed by relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: Clodhoppers here are clumsy rustics rather than heavy boots.
explanation.definitionFit: A clodhopper is a clumsy, unsophisticated person from the country, which is what country bumpkins are.

clue.text: Game with racket and ball played flexibly

definitions.note: rubato is a musical direction, used adverbially

blocks.note: RU is rugby union
a bat is a racket in table tennis
O is shaped like a ball

explanation.surface: A sport with racket and ball, played in a loose way.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all sport, but the definition is musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubato in music means flexible tempo, with the performer speeding up and slowing down for expression.

clue.text: Range of artificial products? Just the wrappers

indicators.note: wrappers are the outside covering, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: outer letters of artificial
outer letters of products

explanation.surface: A line of synthetic goods sold mostly as packaging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' looks like a product range, but it is a mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps are the major mountain range of central Europe.

clue.text: Maybe perfect party in Belfast grew fraught

blocks.note: perfect is an example of a grammatical tense
the DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Things grew tense around an ideal Belfast party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect' looks like praise for the party, but it is the grammatical tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who tensed up became anxious and stressed, which is growing fraught.

clue.text: Person shopping hurried up, back in Primark

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is written bottom to top
the back of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: ran means hurried
last letter of Primark

explanation.surface: A shopper hurried up to the back of a Primark store.
explanation.walkthrough: Primark is a British budget clothes chain; 'shopping' is slang for informing on someone, and a nark is a police informer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nark is British slang for an informer, someone who shops others to the police.

clue.text: Existentialist inspires head of Princeton University?

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the name takes a letter inside
the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: Albert Camus, the French existentialist writer
first letter of Princeton

explanation.surface: An existentialist thinker motivates the president of Princeton.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: a campus stands for the university by association.
explanation.definitionFit: A campus is the grounds and buildings of a university, often used to mean the institution itself.

clue.text: The police agent from America gets stuffed

blocks.note: the police are called the force
a fed is US slang for an FBI agent

explanation.surface: A US agent ends up getting stuffed by the police.
explanation.definitionFit: To be force-fed is to be made to eat, stuffed with food against one's will.
